strengths: Clear motivation and well-structured presentation with informative architecture diagrams
Comprehensive ablation studies examining number of segments, memory size, and memory token necessity
Attention map visualizations providing interpretability of memory read/write patterns across layers
Strong empirical results on Atari games with consistent improvements over baselines
Promised code and weight release supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily applies existing RMT mechanism [31] to Decision Transformer with minor adaptations
Weak MuJoCo results directly contradict main claims—performance equals or underperforms baselines on many tasks (e.g., Walker2d: 84.7 vs 108.1 for DT)
Unfair baseline comparisons: DT evaluated with context length 30 while RMDT uses 3x longer effective context through segments; missing comparison with DT at equivalent context length
No explanation for failure on continuous control or why method requires fundamentally different configurations for different domains (segment overlay, memory fixation for MuJoCo only)

Superficial analysis of when/why memory helps: performance plateaus at 3 segments suggesting modest context needs; attention map analysis is qualitative and doesn't rigorously prove information encoding

Limited Atari evaluation: only 4 environments tested; improvements sometimes modest (Pong: 16.5→17.1 within noise); sources of improvement unclear (context length vs. memory tokens vs. training procedure)
Missing key baselines: no comparison with other memory-augmented RL methods or recent transformer variants for long-context RL
Large standard deviations on MuJoCo tasks (up to ±18.9) suggest instability; statistical significance unclear
Hyperparameter selection process not detailed; environment-specific tuning limits generalizability; no guidance for practitioners on when to use RMDT vs. DT
Computational cost analysis missing: no discussion of training complexity, inference efficiency, or memory overhead of approach
